title: Title
script: Hello everyone, I'm Aicha, a PhD student in social epidemiology at the Sorbonne Public Health Institute in Paris. Today, I'll be talking about childhood sexual violence and smoking in adulthood, using data from a large French cohort.

title: Intro — Inequality
script: Recently, Santé publique France found that 18.2 percent of adults aged 18 to 75 smoke every day. But this isn't spread evenly. Look at this graph: 25 percent of manual workers are daily smokers — compared to only 12 percent in the higher socioeconomic group. This is a well-known inequality. But what about other factors that shape this picture just as strongly — factors we don't usually talk about?

title: Intro — ACE
script: Other factors shape this picture too — such as mental health conditions, migration background, or experiences of adversity in childhood. Adverse childhood experiences are negative experiences occurring before the age of eighteen, which affect children's development, with consequences on mental and physical health in adulthood. But the mechanisms linking this type of trauma to psychoactive substance use remain poorly documented at the population level — specifically for an understudied form of maltreatment: childhood sexual violence.

title: Definition & Prevalence
script: Childhood sexual violence is defined as any sexual act imposed on a person under the age of eighteen, through coercion, manipulation, or abuse of a position of authority. A recent systematic review found that 11 percent of children reported sexual harassment, 9 percent contact sexual violence, and 6 percent forced intercourse. And across the literature, smoking prevalence is consistently reported to be higher among survivors of childhood sexual violence, compared to those who were not exposed.

title: Gaps & Objective
script: But how well is this association actually studied? A few gaps stand out. First, sexual violence is often combined with other adverse experiences into a single cumulative ACE score, rather than studied on its own. Second, existing studies often focus on specific, high-risk populations — such as migrants, incarcerated individuals, military personnel, or children in institutional care — usually with small sample sizes. Third, much of the evidence dates back to studies from around nineteen ninety to twenty ten, with limited recent replication. Finally, tobacco is rarely studied as a standalone outcome — it's usually pooled with other behaviors, such as substance use, obesity, or physical inactivity. So, the objective of this study is: is exposure to childhood sexual violence associated with smoking status in adulthood?

title: Study Population
script: To answer this question, I used data from Constances — one of the largest cohorts in France, with around 220,000 participants aged 18 to 69 at inclusion. Constances allows us to track health over time, and it collects rich data across many domains — lifestyle, environment, occupation, and more.

title: Exposure
script: Childhood sexual violence was assessed using three questions from the Constances questionnaire. The first asked whether someone tried to get the child to touch them sexually. The second asked whether someone subjected the child to sexual touching. And the third asked about forced intercourse. Based on the type and frequency of exposure, we built five categories: no exposure, sexual assault — once or repeated — and forced intercourse — once or repeated.

title: Outcomes
script: We looked at tobacco use two ways. First, how long people have smoked overall — grouped into less than one year, or one year or more. And separately, whether they're still smoking today: never smoked, ex-smoker, or current smoker.

title: Statistical Analyses
script: We used two types of models. For smoking status, we ran two separate binary comparisons — never-smokers versus current smokers, and ex-smokers versus current smokers. For duration of smoking, we used a multinomial model, comparing less than one year, or one year or more, to never having smoked. All models were adjusted for age, origin, education level, parents' socio-occupational category, and other adverse childhood experiences. And all analyses were run separately for women and men.

title: Population Description
script: Our final sample includes just over 102,000 participants. As we saw before, women are strongly overrepresented among those exposed — 76 percent, compared to 52 percent among the non-exposed. Other adverse childhood experiences are also more frequent in the exposed group. Looking at tobacco use, exposed participants show a higher proportion of current smokers, and a lower proportion of never-smokers, compared to non-exposed participants. Age at smoking initiation is very similar between the two groups. Finally, for years of smoking, both categories are more frequent among those exposed: 2.2 percent report less than one year, compared to 1.8 percent among the non-exposed — and 55 percent report one year or more, compared to 46 percent.

title: Results — Duration
script: Let's start with duration of smoking. In panel B — one year or more — the association is clear and consistent: every category of exposure is significantly associated with smoking for a year or more, in both women and men. Panel A — less than one year — tells a different story: the association shows up mainly in women, across most categories, while in men, none of these estimates reach significance.

title: Results — Current Smoking
script: Next: are exposed individuals more likely to be smoking right now, compared to those who never smoked? Here, the pattern is strong and completely consistent: all eight estimates are significant, in both sexes, across all four exposure categories. And the association is clearly stronger for forced intercourse than for sexual assault.

title: Results — Persistent Smoking
script: Finally, among people who have ever smoked, are exposed individuals more likely to still be smoking today, rather than having quit? Here, the picture is narrower: only forced intercourse reaches significance — once, in women; repeated, in men. Sexual assault shows no significant association with difficulty quitting, in either sex.

title: Summary
script: To summarize what we found: smoking is more common among those exposed to childhood sexual violence, across all violence categories. Exposed individuals also report a longer cumulative smoking duration. Shorter reported smoking duration — less than one year — was also associated with exposure, in women specifically. Among those who ever smoked, difficulty quitting is specifically associated with forced intercourse. The association tends to be stronger for forced intercourse than for assault, across models. And this pattern holds for both women and men.

title: Discussion
script: How can we explain this? In our data, exposed individuals are more often current smokers, report a longer smoking duration, and find it harder to quit — especially after forced intercourse. This is consistent with a self-medication explanation. Childhood is a particularly sensitive period: when something as severe as sexual violence happens at that age, it can leave lasting traces — it can interfere with brain, neurobiological, and cognitive development. And in adulthood, that can translate into what we see here: difficulty regulating emotions, and a stronger pull toward coping mechanisms. Of course, this study has limitations. It's cross-sectional, so we can't establish causality. The data is self-reported, with a risk of recall bias. And statistical power is limited for the rarest exposure categories. As a next step, we're currently working on longitudinal trajectories, using repeated measures within the Constances cohort, to help establish temporality.
anchors: more current, longer, harder to quit

title: Conclusion
script: Beyond the well-known social gradient in smoking, our findings point to a largely invisible additional axis of inequality: childhood sexual violence. In France, the CIIVISE — an independent commission on incest and sexual violence against children — has recommended systematic screening for sexual violence across health services since 2023. This isn't yet standard practice — implementation is still ongoing. Integrating trauma screening directly into smoking cessation care could help reach populations that current policy underserves. To conclude: childhood sexual violence is an overlooked dimension of the smoking inequalities this conference set out to address — one that tobacco control and cessation policy may need to account for.

title: Thank You
script: Thank you for your attention — I'm happy to take any questions.
